prompt: A fresh create-next-app scaffold has app/layout.tsx (mostly empty <html>/<body> plus font setup) and app/page.tsx (a Next.js logo, doc links, a deploy button). On day one, before any real feature, what should happen to each?

options.text: Delete the page.tsx demo content down to a placeholder heading; keep layout.tsx even though it looks nearly empty
Delete both files and rebuild layout.tsx from a blank file
Keep both exactly as scaffolded until a real feature specifically requires changing them
Keep page.tsx as reference documentation and delete layout.tsx

hints: Which file is actually doing something (font setup, the <html>/<body> shell) versus which one is just a demo of what routing looks like?
explanation: layout.tsx looks nearly empty but is already doing real work — the document shell, font loading, and the place providers will eventually mount. page.tsx's demo content (logo, doc links) will never be relevant to a real app and is pure disposable weight. Trimming the demo and keeping the plumbing avoids both keeping dead code and rebuilding correctly-configured infrastructure from scratch.

prompt: You're starting a new Next.js app for a tool that, at this moment, does exactly one thing: takes a block of text and summarizes it with Claude. List the top-level folders (beyond what create-next-app already scaffolds) that should exist on day one, and for each one you'd normally expect in a 'real' app but are leaving out for now, say what would have to happen before you'd create it.
hints: Start from what create-next-app already gives you — app/, public/, config files — and ask what's missing to build just this one feature.
A folder like hooks/, services/, or constants/ each need a real reason: a custom hook used more than once, a distinct service layer, a constant referenced from more than one file.
It's fine for the honest answer to be 'no new top-level folders yet' if the one feature doesn't need one.
explanation: A defensible answer: no new top-level folders are needed yet for a single-feature app — app/page.tsx can hold the form and the fetch call directly. lib/ would be created the moment there's a Claude client wrapper worth sharing (e.g. if a second route also needs to call Claude). components/ would be created the moment a chunk of JSX has an independent identity worth extracting (per this module's second lesson). hooks/, services/, types/, constants/ each wait for their own specific trigger — a reused custom hook, a distinct service boundary, a shared type, a constant used in two places — none of which exist yet in a one-feature app.

prompt: A page.tsx renders a form (state, submit handler, fields) followed by a <ul> of items, where each <li> renders one Brief's title, summary, and deliverable count. Which piece is the strongest candidate to extract into its own component right now?

options.text: The <li> block — it takes one Brief and renders it, independent of the form's state around it
The whole file, wrapped in a single <PageContent /> component
Nothing yet — wait until the file exceeds 200 lines
The form's submit handler alone, without its fields

hints: Which chunk of JSX would you be able to describe in one sentence without mentioning the form at all?
explanation: The <li> block has a self-contained identity — a Brief in, JSX out — that doesn't depend on the form's state or handlers. That's the actual test for a good extraction, not file length (which would justify wrapping everything in a PageContent shell that changes nothing) and not an arbitrary line-count threshold.

prompt: A teammate 'refactors' a 200-line page.tsx into an 8-line page.tsx that renders <PageContent /> plus a 195-line PageContent.tsx containing everything the original file had, unchanged, just moved. Explain in your own words why this doesn't reduce complexity, and describe what a real extraction from the same file would look like instead.
hints: Ask what PageContent.tsx does, in one sentence, without saying 'the rest of the page.'
Look for a chunk of JSX inside it with an identity independent of the rest — a list item, a card, a repeated form field.
A real extraction gives that independent chunk its own typed props interface.
explanation: The refactor doesn't help because nothing was decomposed — the same six tangled concerns (form state, fetch logic, error display, list rendering, etc.) just moved to a new file wholesale, with an extra import required to find them. A real extraction would instead identify something with independent identity inside that tangle — e.g. the <li> rendering one Brief — and give it its own component with a typed props interface, leaving page.tsx (or PageContent) composing clearly-named pieces instead of hiding one undivided block behind a new filename.

prompt: BriefList and WeeklyCount each independently fetch and store their own copy of the briefs array. Submitting a new brief updates BriefList's copy but not WeeklyCount's, so the count goes stale. What's the actual mechanism causing this?

options.text: There are two separate useState copies of the same fact, with nothing keeping them in sync when one changes
React fails to re-render sibling components together
WeeklyCount's fetch request is intermittently failing
useState doesn't support arrays reliably

hints: WeeklyCount's own fetch worked fine on mount — the bug isn't in that fetch. What happens after mount?
explanation: WeeklyCount fetched once, correctly, and then never again — nothing tells it the underlying data changed, because as far as it knows it holds the current, complete truth in its own state. The fix isn't a better fetch or a React workaround; it's removing the duplication by lifting the shared array to a common ancestor so there's exactly one copy.

prompt: briefdesk adds a logged-in user's display name, needed by the header, the footer, and a settings page — none of which are near each other in the component tree. Separately, it adds a 'currently selected brief' used by three components all nested inside the same detail page. Explain which of these two should use Context and which should just lift state to a common parent, and why the difference isn't simply 'more than one consumer.'
hints: For each case, ask: is there a nearby common ancestor that isn't effectively the whole app?
The selected-brief case has three consumers all inside one page — a genuinely local common ancestor.
The user's name has consumers with no shared parent except the app root itself.
explanation: The selected brief should be lifted to its page's state and passed as props — its three consumers are all nested inside one nearby page, so prop-passing costs almost nothing and stays easy to trace. The user's name is the real case for Context: its consumers (header, footer, a separate settings page) have no useful common ancestor short of the entire app, so threading it through every intervening layer as props would mean many components that don't care about the user's name still having to pass it along. The deciding factor is how far apart the consumers are and whether a nearby ancestor exists — not simply whether more than one component needs the value.

prompt: briefdesk's brief detail view is currently shown by conditionally rendering different JSX based on a selectedBrief state variable on the main page. What's the strongest reason to give it its own route instead?

options.text: A user would plausibly want to bookmark, share, or send a direct link to a specific brief's detail view
Routes are always better practice than conditional rendering, regardless of the use case
It makes the component tree shallower
It removes the need for any state at all in the detail view

hints: Would someone ever want to send a client or teammate a link straight to this exact brief?
explanation: The deciding test is whether the state is something a user would want to bookmark, share, or navigate to directly — a specific brief's detail view clearly passes that test (sending a client a direct link is a real use case), which a query-toggle for something like a sort order would not. Routes aren't inherently better than conditional state; they're the right tool specifically when a URL would provide real value.

prompt: briefdesk's /briefs/[id] route handles both viewing and editing a brief, switched by a ?edit=true query param inside one page.tsx file. Rewrite this as proper file-based routes using the App Router's conventions, and explain one concrete thing the split gains you that the query-param version couldn't have.
hints: Use a nested edit/ folder under [id]/ with its own page.tsx.
Each route folder can have its own loading.tsx and error.tsx picked up automatically.
Think about what's different between viewing and editing: loading behavior, error handling, or the URL itself.
explanation:
```
app/briefs/[id]/page.tsx        # /briefs/123       — view
app/briefs/[id]/loading.tsx      # loading state for viewing
app/briefs/[id]/edit/page.tsx      # /briefs/123/edit   — edit
app/briefs/[id]/edit/loading.tsx    # loading state for editing
```
Splitting into two routes means each screen gets its own loading.tsx and error.tsx boundary automatically, instead of both screens having to share whatever loading/error handling was written into the one combined file — an edit form's loading state (fields populating from data that might still be in flight) can now be handled independently of the view page's. The URL also becomes self-describing: /briefs/123/edit says what it is without needing to inspect a query string.

prompt: briefdesk has exactly one brief type. A teammate proposes building a generic, config-driven BriefTypeRenderer now, so 'adding a new type later is just a config change.' What's the strongest objection to building it at this point?

options.text: The config schema is a guess made from zero real examples of what actually varies between brief types
Config-driven components are always worse than code-driven ones
Next.js doesn't support config-driven rendering patterns
It would make the app slower at runtime

hints: With one brief type in existence, is there any real evidence yet for which parts of a 'brief type' actually vary?
explanation: The problem isn't that config-driven rendering is a bad pattern in general — it's that with only one real brief type in existence, there's no evidence yet for which fields genuinely vary between types and which stay fixed. Whatever schema gets picked is a guess, and if it's wrong, the second brief type becomes two entangled problems (fit an unverified schema, or change the schema) instead of one simple one (write the second type's code).

prompt: Once briefdesk has three real brief-type view components (ProjectBriefView, LogoBriefView, WebsiteBriefView), each with slightly different section content but the same outer <article><h1> shell, write the shared BriefView component they should be refactored into, and explain what specifically makes this abstraction different from the config-driven guess proposed with only one brief type.
hints: Identify what's identical across all three real components (the shell) versus what varies (the sections' labels and content).
The shared component should take the varying part as a typed parameter — an array of {title, content} sections.
The difference from the earlier guess is that this shape comes from three verified real cases, not zero or one.

prompt: A scaffolded Vite + React app still has its default App.css with a spinning logo animation, three weeks into building a real invoice-tracking tool. What's the right move?

options.text: Delete the demo styles and animation — they're disposable scaffolding, not load-bearing
Keep them; deleting default styles risks breaking the build
Leave them until the app is feature-complete, then clean up in one pass

hints: Is the spinning logo doing any real work for an invoice tracker, three weeks in?
explanation: Demo content that's had three weeks to prove it's irrelevant should go — 'clean up later' is how a codebase accumulates dead weight nobody remembers the origin of. Deleting unused CSS classes doesn't break a build; the build doesn't care whether a class is referenced.

prompt: A new project creates services/, repositories/, adapters/, and dto/ folders on day one, before any feature exists, because 'that's proper layered architecture.' Two features in, three of the four folders are still empty. What does this cost, specifically?

options.text: Every new file now has more plausible homes than the app's actual size justifies, and empty folders don't reflect anything real yet
Nothing — empty folders cost zero bytes and can be safely ignored
It's purely a matter of taste with no real downside either way

hints: If a new contributor asks 'where does this go,' does an empty folder answer that question or just add options?
explanation: An empty folder isn't neutral — it's a guess about a future structure that hasn't arrived, and in the meantime it adds a decision every new file has to make ('does this go in services/ or adapters/?') without any real precedent to base that decision on.

prompt: A `<ProductCard>` component takes a single `product` prop, renders an image, a name, and a price, and is used in exactly one place — a product grid. A teammate says it's premature to have extracted it since it's only used once. Is that right?

options.text: No — reuse count isn't the test; the card has an independent identity (product in, JSX out) regardless of how many places currently render it
Yes — nothing should be extracted into its own component until it's used in at least two places
It depends only on the component's line count

hints: Could you describe what ProductCard does in one sentence without mentioning the grid around it?
explanation: Independent identity, not reuse count, is the test this module actually teaches — a component that takes one clear input and renders one clear thing is a reasonable extraction even with a single call site, especially once it's likely to be reused (a detail page, a search result) even if that hasn't happened yet.

prompt: A stale-count bug like WeeklyCount's is reported. Put these diagnostic and fix steps in the order you'd actually do them.

items: Confirm both components are independently fetching/storing what's conceptually the same data
Notice the symptom: one component reflects an update, a sibling doesn't
Identify the nearest common ancestor of the two components
Lift the shared state to that ancestor and pass it down as props
Remove the now-redundant local fetch/state from both children

hints: You notice the bug before you know the cause; you diagnose duplicated state before you know where to lift it to.
explanation: You start from the observed symptom, then confirm the actual mechanism (two copies of one fact), then find where those two components actually converge in the tree, then move the state there, then clean up the now-dead local copies. Skipping the diagnosis step and jumping straight to 'add Context everywhere' is the mistake this module warns against.

prompt: A settings toggle for 'compact list view' changes how items render on a dashboard. Should this toggle's state live in the URL as a route or query param?

options.text: Not necessarily — ask whether a user would plausibly want to bookmark or share that specific toggle state; if not, plain component state (or localStorage) is fine
Yes, always — any state affecting what's rendered belongs in the URL for consistency
No, never — the URL should only ever represent navigation between pages, never settings

hints: Would someone send a teammate a link specifically because it's in 'compact view'?
explanation: The test is whether the state is something worth bookmarking or sharing — a display preference like compact-view usually isn't (it's a personal preference, better suited to localStorage than a URL), while a specific record's detail view usually is. Neither blanket rule ('always in the URL' or 'never in the URL') survives contact with real cases.

prompt: A team builds a generic, plugin-style `<ReportRenderer plugin={reportConfig} />` before writing a single real report — planning to support 'any report type' through configuration. Diagnose what's wrong with the timing, and describe what they should build instead right now.
hints: With zero real reports built, what evidence exists for what a config schema needs to express?
What would the rule of three suggest building first instead?
Contrast this with the BriefView example, which was built from three real components.
explanation: With zero real reports in existence, the plugin config schema is a pure guess — there's no evidence yet for which parts of a report genuinely vary and which are fixed. The team should instead build the first real report as straightforward code, then a second one as straightforward code too (even duplicating structure from the first if needed), and only extract a shared abstraction on the third real report, once the actual pattern of what varies and what's fixed is visible from real cases rather than assumed in advance.

prompt: Two features in a dashboard app now have near-identical filter-panel JSX, duplicated rather than shared. True or false: this duplication is a bug that should be fixed the moment it's noticed.

config.statement: Duplication between exactly two real, similar features should always be extracted into a shared abstraction as soon as it's noticed.
config.rubric: A full answer explains that two data points usually aren't enough to know which parts of the pattern are genuinely shared versus coincidentally similar, and that a third real case is what actually reveals the true shape worth abstracting.

hints: What does the rule of three say about the second occurrence of a pattern, specifically?
explanation: False. Duplication between exactly two real cases is often the cheaper, more honest choice — it's visible, easy to change independently if the two cases diverge further, and avoids abstracting from too little evidence. The rule of three exists precisely because the second occurrence usually isn't enough data to know which parts of the pattern are genuinely shared; forcing an abstraction at two data points risks the same guessed-schema problem as abstracting from one.

prompt: A React app reads process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and calls Claude directly from a client component. No key is ever logged anywhere. Why is it still exposed to every visitor?

options.text: NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are inlined directly into the JavaScript bundle every browser downloads, readable in devtools regardless of logging
It isn't actually exposed unless someone specifically searches for it
It's only exposed to visitors on the same WiFi network
It's exposed only if the developer console is left open

hints: What does the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix specifically instruct the Next.js build process to do?
explanation: NEXT_PUBLIC_ is a documented Next.js convention that inlines a variable's value into the client-side JavaScript at build time — it exists for genuinely public values. Using it for a secret means the secret is sitting in plain text in the deployed bundle, discoverable by opening browser devtools' Sources tab, with no logging, breach, or special access required.

prompt: Explain, beyond hiding the API key, what having a server-side route handler in the request path enables that a browser calling Claude directly cannot do — name at least two concrete things.
hints: Think about what a server can check or enforce before a request even reaches Claude.
Think about what's needed for streaming, retries, or rate limiting to work at all.
explanation: A server-side route handler can validate a request before ever calling Claude (rejecting empty or oversized input), fix cost-relevant parameters like model and max_tokens so a client can't override them, and provide a single trustworthy position to implement rate limiting across users — none of which a browser calling Claude directly has any shared, trustworthy place to do. It's also the only position from which streaming, timeouts, and retries (this module's later lessons) can be implemented at all.

prompt: A route handler does `const message = await client.messages.create(await req.json())` and returns the raw message object to the browser unmodified. What's the strongest objection to this, beyond it 'just being sloppy'?

options.text: The browser controls every field Anthropic's API accepts (including model and max_tokens), and the frontend now depends on Anthropic's exact response shape instead of a contract briefdesk owns
This will throw a runtime error because req.json() can't be passed directly into messages.create
Nothing is wrong with this as long as the route is only ever called from briefdesk's own frontend

hints: What happens if someone sends a request body with a different model field, or an inflated max_tokens?
explanation: Forwarding the raw body means the server never decides what's actually allowed — a client (or a modified request from browser devtools) can request an expensive model or an uncapped token count, with the server offering no resistance. And returning Anthropic's raw response ties the frontend to an external API's internal shape, which can change independent of briefdesk's own releases.

prompt: A route's catch block currently does `return Response.json(err)`, forwarding Anthropic's raw error object straight to the browser. Rewrite this so the browser gets a stable, plain-language error, and explain where the raw error detail should still go.
hints: The raw error is still useful — just not to the browser.
Pick a status code the frontend can branch on without parsing provider-specific error text.
Match the register from the CLI errors module: what happened, in language the actual reader can act on.

prompt: briefdesk's non-streamed brief generation takes 8-14 seconds. Streaming is added, and the total time to fully finish is still 8-14 seconds. What did streaming actually fix?

options.text: It changed a long silent wait into continuously visible progress — the user sees text growing immediately instead of nothing until the very end
Nothing — if total time is unchanged, streaming provided no real benefit
It reduced the number of tokens Claude needed to generate

hints: What does the user actually see during those 8-14 seconds, with and without streaming?
explanation: Streaming doesn't touch total generation time — the same 8-14 seconds elapses either way. What changes is that the first visible words arrive in under a second, and text keeps growing throughout, instead of twelve seconds of nothing followed by everything appearing at once. That's the entire fix for a response that otherwise reads as frozen.

prompt: Write the client-side code that reads a streaming SSE response from /api/brief and appends each chunk of text to a `brief` state variable as it arrives, instead of waiting for the full response with res.json().
hints: Get a reader with res.body.getReader() and loop reading chunks until done is true.
Decode each chunk, split on newlines, and filter for lines starting with 'data: '.
Append each parsed chunk to existing state rather than replacing it.

prompt: A Claude call in briefdesk's route handler has no timeout set. A request hangs for ten minutes with no response either way. What's the actual missing piece?

options.text: An explicit timeout — without one, the request has no self-imposed deadline and can wait far longer than any real user experience should tolerate
A retry loop — retries would have made this resolve faster
A bigger max_tokens value

hints: If the request had a 30-second timeout, would it still be able to hang for ten minutes?
explanation: Without an explicit timeout, a stalled connection has no deadline distinguishing it from a request that's simply taking its time — nothing tells the SDK to give up after a bounded, predictable interval. A retry wouldn't help a request that's still pending; the fix is capping how long any single attempt is allowed to wait in the first place.

prompt: Sort each Claude API failure into whether a second identical attempt has a genuine chance of succeeding.

items.text: 429 — rate limited
529 — API temporarily overloaded
401 — invalid API key
400 — malformed request body
A dropped connection mid-request
403 — the account lacks access to the requested model

hints: Ask: did the specific thing causing this failure change between attempt one and attempt two, with nothing else changing?
explanation: 429 and 529 are conditions that can genuinely clear between attempts — too much traffic right now doesn't mean too much traffic in 500ms. A dropped connection is often a one-off network blip worth one more try. 401, 400, and 403 are all facts about the request or credentials themselves — nothing about retrying changes an invalid key, a malformed body, or a model the account can't access, so a retry just delays an identical failure.

prompt: briefdesk relies only on Anthropic's account-level rate limit to protect against excess usage. A frontend bug fires the same Claude call on every keystroke for four minutes. Why doesn't Anthropic's limit stop this quickly?

options.text: Anthropic's limit is scoped to the whole account across all users — one buggy tab can generate real, fully billed cost long before that account-wide ceiling is reached
Anthropic doesn't enforce rate limits on paid accounts
Rate limits only apply to requests made outside business hours

hints: Is Anthropic's limit measuring one user's behavior, or the account's total traffic?
explanation: Anthropic's rate limit protects Anthropic's infrastructure at the whole-account level — it has no concept of 'this one user is misbehaving,' and every call under that ceiling is fully billed regardless. A per-user limit that briefdesk enforces itself is the only thing that catches this quickly.

prompt: briefdesk's real usage logs show a designer typically generates a new brief every 15-40 seconds during a working session. A teammate wants to set the rate limit to 1 request per minute 'to be safe.' Explain what's wrong with that number and propose a better one, with reasoning.
hints: Convert 15-40 seconds per brief into requests per minute at a normal working pace.
Consider how quickly a runaway bug (firing on every keystroke) would hit a limit of 1/minute versus a slightly higher one.
The right number should leave headroom above real usage while still catching a bug within a second or two, not a full minute.
explanation: A brief every 15-40 seconds is roughly 2-4 requests per minute at a normal pace, so a limit of 1/minute would block a real, non-buggy working session almost immediately — actively breaking the tool for legitimate use. A limit around 5-8/minute comfortably covers real usage with headroom, while still catching a bug firing many times per second within a second or two, since that bug would blow past even a limit of 6 almost instantly. The number should come from real usage data, not a round number chosen for how cautious it sounds.

prompt: A team stores their Claude key in a `.env.local` file with the variable name `REACT_APP_CLAUDE_KEY` for a Create React App project, then calls the Anthropic SDK directly inside a component. Is the naming convention the problem here?

options.text: No — REACT_APP_ prefixed variables are Create React App's equivalent of NEXT_PUBLIC_, also inlined into the client bundle; the real problem is calling Claude from the client at all, regardless of variable naming
Yes — renaming it to something without REACT_APP_ would fix the exposure
No — REACT_APP_ variables stay server-side in Create React App

hints: Does Create React App have its own convention for which env vars get bundled into client code?
explanation: REACT_APP_ is Create React App's version of the same mechanism NEXT_PUBLIC_ provides in Next.js — any variable with that prefix gets bundled into the client JavaScript. Simply renaming the variable wouldn't fix anything if the call is still happening from a client component; the fix is moving the Claude call to a server (an Express backend, a serverless function) regardless of what the variable is named.

prompt: A route handler forwards the browser's entire request body into messages.create(), including whatever `system` prompt the client sends. What's the risk specific to letting the client set the system prompt?

options.text: A client could override the intended system prompt entirely, changing the tool's behavior or bypassing constraints the server meant to enforce
There's no risk — system prompts are always safe for a client to set
It would cause a type error, since system must be set server-side

hints: What is the system prompt normally used for, and what happens if a user can simply replace it?
explanation: The system prompt is often where an app's actual behavioral constraints and instructions live — letting a client set it arbitrarily means those constraints can be replaced or removed entirely by anyone who inspects the request and modifies it, defeating whatever the system prompt was meant to enforce.

prompt: Put these steps in the order they'd actually happen when adding streaming to a previously non-streamed Claude route.

items: Replace client.messages.create() with client.messages.stream()
Wrap the stream in a ReadableStream, enqueueing each text chunk as an SSE data: line
Set Content-Type: text/event-stream on the Response
Update the client to read res.body via getReader() instead of res.json()
Confirm text visibly grows in the UI instead of appearing all at once

hints: The server side has to actually stream before the client can read a stream — and the client fix has to happen before you can verify the UI update.
explanation: The server-side pieces come first: switch to the streaming SDK method, wrap it for the Response, and set the right header — none of that is visible until the client is also updated to read progressively instead of waiting for the whole body. Verifying the visible result is necessarily last, since it depends on every earlier step being correct.

prompt: A route sets `timeout: 5000` (5 seconds) on every Claude call, including ones generating a genuinely long document that reliably takes 20+ seconds. Users report the feature 'just breaks' on longer documents. What's the actual mistake?

options.text: The timeout is shorter than the legitimate, expected duration for this specific kind of call — it's cutting off requests that were working correctly, not catching stalled ones
Timeouts should never be set below 60 seconds for any Claude call
Nothing is wrong — a short timeout is always safer

hints: What's the difference between 'safe' and 'correctly calibrated to what this specific call actually needs'?
explanation: A timeout needs to be longer than the legitimate, expected duration of the call it's guarding — otherwise it fails requests that were working exactly as intended, which is a different and worse problem than the hang it was meant to prevent. The fix isn't 'no timeout' or 'always short' — it's setting the number based on what this specific request genuinely needs.

prompt: A retry function retries every failed Claude call exactly 3 times with no check on the error type. Rewrite the retry condition so a 400 (malformed request) fails immediately on the first attempt, while a 429 gets up to 3 attempts with backoff.
hints: Check err.status (or the equivalent field on the SDK's error type) before deciding to retry.
A 400 should throw immediately, not enter the retry loop at all.

prompt: A team sets a rate limit of 100 requests per minute per user on their Claude-backed endpoint, 'to be generous.' Their logs show real users average 1 request every 20-30 seconds. What's the actual problem with 100/minute?

options.text: It's so far above real usage that it would barely slow down a runaway bug or bad actor — the limit exists to catch abnormal behavior, and 100/minute doesn't distinguish normal from abnormal here
There's no problem — a generous limit is always safer for user experience
100/minute is technically impossible for any API to enforce

hints: If real usage is roughly 2-3 requests per minute, what would it take for a bug to actually hit a 100/minute ceiling?
explanation: A limit set far above real usage still technically works as a ceiling, but it fails at the actual job of a rate limit here — catching a bug or abuse quickly. A runaway loop firing many times per second would still generate a large number of billed calls before ever approaching 100 in a minute. The number needs to be close enough to real usage that abnormal behavior actually trips it fast.

prompt: Match each web-app Claude-integration mistake to the lesson from this module it violates.

pairs.right: Why the API key can never reach the browser

pairs.left: A route returning Anthropic's raw message object unmodified
pairs.right: A minimal server route that proxies the call

pairs.left: A UI showing nothing for 12 seconds then all text at once
pairs.right: Streaming a response into the UI as it arrives

pairs.left: A retry loop that retries a 400 three times
pairs.right: Timeouts, retries and a request that never finishes

pairs.left: A limit of 100/minute when real usage is 2-3/minute
pairs.right: Rate limiting your own endpoint before someone else costs you money

hints: Match each scenario to the specific lesson whose core lesson it directly violates, not just a generally related one.
explanation: Each mistake maps to the lesson that specifically diagnoses it: an exposed key is the browser-exposure lesson; an unshaped response is the proxy-contract lesson; a silent 12-second wait is the streaming lesson; retrying a non-retryable error is the timeouts-and-retries lesson; and an oversized limit is the rate-limiting lesson, since it fails to catch abnormal usage the way a correctly-sized one would.

prompt: A settings screen has a page title, a "Save changes" button, and eight labeled form fields, all rendered at the same 15px, gray-800, font-weight 400. A user reports "I can't tell what I'm supposed to do here." What's the most direct fix?

options.text: Give "Save changes" clearly higher visual weight (size, color, or contrast) than the surrounding labels and fields, so it reads as the obvious next step
Reduce the number of form fields from eight to four so there's less to look at
Increase the font size of all nine elements uniformly so everything is easier to read
Add a paragraph above the form explaining what the screen is for

hints: The complaint isn't that the screen is unreadable — it's that nothing signals which element is the one to act on.
Uniform changes (bigger text everywhere, fewer fields) don't create contrast between elements — hierarchy needs difference, not uniformity.
explanation: The confusion isn't about legibility or field count — it's that nothing on the screen is visually louder than anything else, so there's no signal for what to do once the fields are filled in. Making every element bigger together (or explaining it in prose) doesn't create the contrast that's actually missing; giving the one action the user needs to take (Save changes) genuinely higher visual weight than the surrounding labels does.

prompt: A briefdesk screen has three buttons in a row, all styled as solid bg-blue-600: "Generate brief", "Export as PDF", and "Share link". Diagnose what's wrong with this, and rewrite the styling so the hierarchy matches how often and how centrally each action is actually used (generating a brief is the core, constant action; exporting and sharing are occasional, secondary ones).
hints: Three identically-styled buttons means the user's eye has three equally loud options and no signal for which matters most.
Keep the solid color for the one action that's core to the screen; move the other two to a lighter treatment — an outline or a plain text link.
explanation: Three solid-blue buttons of equal weight give the eye nowhere obvious to land, even though each individual button is legible on its own — the problem is they all compete at the same volume. Generate brief is the action this screen exists for, so it keeps the solid `bg-blue-600` treatment; Export as PDF and Share link are real but occasional actions, so they'd move to `border border-gray-300 text-gray-700` outlined buttons or plain text links, visibly stepping back from the primary action without disappearing entirely.

prompt: A codebase has four different border-radius values in use — rounded-sm, rounded, rounded-md, rounded-lg — applied to buttons seemingly at random depending on who wrote each one. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: There's no single shared decision for "button radius" — each button was styled independently instead of referencing one fixed choice
Buttons in different parts of the app are supposed to look different, and this is working as intended
Tailwind's rounded utilities are buggy and shouldn't be trusted for consistency

hints: Four different values on the *same kind* of element (buttons) applied seemingly at random is the signature of drift, not intentional variation.
explanation: Four different radii on buttons specifically, with no apparent reasoning, is the classic signature of missing shared tokens — each person styled their own button without a single documented answer for "what radius do buttons use." This isn't a Tailwind reliability issue; the utilities work exactly as specified, there just isn't a fixed decision behind which one gets used.

prompt: You're starting a new small app. List the five design-system decisions you'd fix on day one, and for each one give the actual value you'd pick (not just the category) — e.g. not just "a primary color" but which color.
hints: The five categories are: type scale, color pair (primary + neutral), spacing scale, border-radius, shadow.

It's fine to reuse Tailwind's sensible defaults (its default spacing scale, its default gray palette) rather than inventing custom values for everything — the point is fixing the decision, not necessarily customizing it.
explanation: A defensible answer names all five: (1) a type scale of maybe 4 sizes — text-sm/base/xl/2xl and nothing else; (2) a primary color (e.g. blue-600) plus Tailwind's default gray scale for neutrals, with no other colors introduced until a real use case (a danger state, a success toast) needs one; (3) Tailwind's default spacing scale used as-is rather than arbitrary pixel values; (4) one radius, e.g. rounded-md, for anything that isn't a pill-shaped badge; (5) one shadow, e.g. shadow-sm, for any elevated surface. The specific values matter less than the fact that each one is a single, named, written-down decision rather than left to whoever builds the next component.

prompt: A component has `const [items, setItems] = useState<Item[]>([])` and renders `items.map(...)` directly, with no other state. What's the direct consequence of this, before any fetch resolves?

options.text: The screen renders identically to a genuinely empty result — there's no way to distinguish "still loading" from "loaded and empty" from the rendered output
React throws a runtime error because items is empty on first render
The component automatically shows a default browser loading spinner
Nothing — this is the correct way to represent a loading state

hints: What does items.map render when items is []? Now compare that to what it renders once the fetch resolves with a genuinely empty result.
explanation: Both "hasn't fetched yet" and "fetched, and there's genuinely nothing there" produce the exact same visible output — nothing — because there's only one state variable representing both situations. React doesn't throw on an empty array, and there's no automatic loading UI; the fix is an explicit status value alongside the data.

prompt: Match each empty-state cause in briefdesk to the call-to-action that actually addresses it.

pairs.left: A brand-new account with zero briefs ever created
pairs.right: "Generate your first brief" button pointing at /new

pairs.left: A search for "logo" matched none of the account's 40 real briefs
pairs.right: "Clear filters" button, plus a note that the search didn't match anything

pairs.left: The account just deleted its only remaining brief
pairs.right: "Undo delete" option, or at minimum copy that doesn't imply the account has never had any briefs

right: A generic "Something went wrong, try again" retry button
A link to briefdesk's pricing page

hints: Match each cause to the action that's actually true for that situation — not a generic message that would technically apply to all three.
explanation: Each cause implies a different honest next step: a truly new account should be pointed toward creating its first brief; a filtered-to-zero search should be pointed toward clearing the filter, not starting over; a just-emptied account (previously had briefs) shouldn't be told to "generate your first one" as if it's starting from scratch. The distractors — a generic error retry and a pricing link — don't match any of the three causes, which is exactly the kind of mismatch a single one-size-fits-all empty state produces.

prompt: A card grid is written as `className="grid grid-cols-3 gap-4"` with no responsive prefixes. What happens on a 375px-wide phone, and what's the mobile-first fix?

options.text: Three columns render at every width, including 375px, squeezing each card to roughly 100px wide; the fix is `grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3` so the column count scales up with available width
Tailwind automatically caps grid-cols-3 at one column below 768px with no changes needed
Nothing breaks — grid-cols-3 only takes effect on screens wide enough to fit three columns
The fix is switching from CSS grid to flexbox, which handles narrow screens automatically

hints: An unprefixed Tailwind class applies at every screen width unless a breakpoint prefix overrides it starting at some width.
The fix isn't a different layout system — it's adding responsive prefixes to the same grid classes.
explanation: Unprefixed Tailwind classes are the default at every viewport width — there's no automatic narrow-screen cap. `grid-cols-3` at 375px genuinely renders three roughly-100px columns. The mobile-first fix keeps the same grid approach but scopes the column count to breakpoints, starting from one column as the unprefixed default and adding columns as width increases — not a switch to a different layout primitive.

prompt: Sort each mobile UI decision into whether it passes or fails a one-handed, lying-down usability check.

items.text: A 44px-tall primary action button pinned near the bottom of the screen
A 20px close (X) icon in the extreme top-left corner of a tall screen, with no padding around it
Two adjacent icon buttons, 'Archive' and 'Delete forever', both 24px, with 2px between them
A 48px 'Save' button with 12px of margin separating it from the next control

hints: Check both size (roughly 44px minimum) and position (bottom/center reaches easier than top corners for a one-handed hold) for each item.
A destructive action sitting immediately next to a routine one, both small, fails even before considering size alone.
explanation: The 44px bottom-pinned button and the 48px Save button with real margin both meet the size-and-spacing bar and sit in a reachable zone. The 20px unpadded corner icon fails on both size and position — small and in the hardest-to-reach spot for a one-handed hold. The adjacent Archive/Delete pair fails on size (24px, under the ~44px guidance) and on adjacency — a destructive action right next to a routine one at that size is an easy mis-tap.

prompt: A four-step checkout flow shows steady 15% drop-off at every single step, and a visual redesign of all four screens didn't change the numbers. True or false: the next thing worth trying is another round of visual polish, done more carefully this time.

config.statement: Given steady drop-off across every step that a visual redesign didn't move, another round of visual polish is the right next experiment.
config.rubric: A full answer explains that even drop-off unmoved by visual changes points at step count as the friction, and that the next experiment worth trying is reducing or merging steps, not a second visual pass.

hints: The first redesign was a real, presumably well-executed visual pass, and the numbers didn't move — what does that already rule out?
explanation: False. The evidence — steady, even drop-off, unchanged by an actual visual redesign — already tested the "make it look better" hypothesis and it didn't move the number. Trying a second round of the same kind of fix is unlikely to work for the same reason the first round didn't: the friction isn't in how any individual step looks, it's in there being four separate decision points at all. The next experiment worth running is reducing the step count.

prompt: A project-management tool's "create workspace" flow asks, in order: workspace name, workspace logo upload, team size selector, industry dropdown, and then finally lets the user create their first task. Identify which fields genuinely block creating a first task, and describe where the rest should move to instead of being removed from the product entirely.
hints: Ask, for each field: does the first task-creation screen actually need this value to exist, or does the app just currently require it out of habit?

Deferred data can move to a settings screen, an optional post-signup prompt, or a moment later in the flow where it's actually used (e.g. industry might matter for a template suggestion, not for creating a task).
explanation: Only "workspace name" is plausibly load-bearing — a task needs a workspace to belong to, and a workspace needs some identifier. Logo upload, team size, and industry are all real, useful data the product might want, but none of them are required for a first task to exist. A defensible redesign: ask for the workspace name, create the workspace, and drop the user straight into task creation; move logo upload to workspace settings (most teams add a logo eventually, not before their first task); move team size and industry to an optional one-question prompt shown after the first task is created, or infer/ask for them only at the moment they'd actually change behavior — e.g. industry mattering when suggesting a template.

prompt: A pricing page has three plan cards, each with a "Choose plan" button styled identically — same solid blue, same size. The team wants users to notice the middle ("Pro") plan as the recommended one. What should change?

options.text: Give the Pro card's button (and possibly the card itself — a border, a "Most popular" badge) higher visual weight than the other two, which step back to a lighter treatment
Make all three buttons larger so the whole page feels more prominent
Leave the buttons identical — the plan names alone should communicate which is recommended

hints: Three identically-styled buttons give the eye no signal about which one the business wants noticed.
explanation: Identical styling across all three buttons treats them as equally weighted, which contradicts the actual goal of steering attention toward one plan. Making all three bigger preserves the same lack of contrast at a larger scale. The fix is the same hierarchy principle from this module's first lesson: give the one option that matters most a visibly higher weight, and let the others recede.

prompt: A codebase has shadow-sm on cards, a custom `0 2px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.08)` on dropdowns, and shadow-md on modals — three different shadow values for three different "elevated surface" components. Per this module's five-decision system, is this a problem?

options.text: Yes — this is exactly the kind of drift the five-decision system exists to prevent; one shadow value should cover all elevated surfaces unless there's a real reason to distinguish them
No — every component type deserves its own custom shadow tuned to its specific size and content
It only matters if a user complains about it

hints: Compare this to the four-radii-on-buttons example from the lesson — is there a stated reason for the difference, or does it look like three people made three independent choices?
explanation: Without a stated reason for the difference (unlike badges deliberately being rounded-full while buttons are rounded-md), three separate shadow values on the same category of thing — "something elevated above the page" — is drift, not intentional design. The five-decision system exists precisely so that "what shadow do elevated surfaces use" has one findable answer.

prompt: A team is fixing a list screen that flashes blank before showing content, then shows an unhelpful generic empty state after filtering. Put these fix steps in the order they'd actually happen.

items: Notice the blank flash and the wrong empty-state copy after filtering
Add an explicit 'loading' | 'empty' | 'loaded' status instead of relying on the empty-array default
Identify the different causes of 'empty' the screen can actually have (first-time, filtered-to-zero)
Write distinct copy and calls-to-action for each cause
Verify the loading state, and each empty-state variant, by triggering them deliberately

hints: Fixing the missing loading state and diagnosing the empty-state causes are two separate problems from this module — do them as two passes, not tangled together.
explanation: You start from the observed symptom, then fix the structural gap (no explicit loading state) before addressing content (which empty-state copy to show), since the copy work depends on first identifying the distinct causes. Verifying by deliberately triggering each state — not just reloading and hoping to catch it — closes the loop the same way this module's lessons treated both loading and empty as designed, not accidental, states.

prompt: A three-column dashboard is written entirely with grid-cols-3, no responsive prefixes. On a 390px phone the columns are roughly 120px wide. What's the correct mobile-first rewrite?

options.text: grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3 — start at one column as the unprefixed default, add columns as width increases
grid-cols-3 lg:grid-cols-1 — keep three columns as the default and reduce to one only on large screens
Remove the grid entirely and use only inline styles for width

hints: Mobile-first means the unprefixed class is the narrow-screen default, and wider-screen classes are the overrides layered on top — not the other way around.
explanation: The second option inverts the direction Tailwind's breakpoints work in — `lg:` only applies at large widths and above, so `grid-cols-3 lg:grid-cols-1` would still show three columns on the phone (unprefixed, applies everywhere) and switch to one column only on large screens, the opposite of what's needed. The correct fix keeps grid but scopes the column count with prefixes going the right direction: fewest columns as the unprefixed default, more added at wider breakpoints.

prompt: Match each mobile UI issue to the specific fix that addresses it (not a generic "make it bigger").

pairs.left: A 22px icon button with no padding, hard to tap accurately
pairs.right: Increase the tappable area to roughly 44px, even if the icon itself stays visually small (padding counts toward the target)

pairs.left: A primary action button placed at the very top of a tall screen
pairs.right: Move it to the bottom of the screen, or pin it, so a one-handed thumb reaches it without a grip shift

pairs.left: Two visually similar icon buttons ('Duplicate' and 'Delete') placed directly adjacent
pairs.right: Separate them spatially, or require a confirming second step before the destructive one executes

right: Switch the whole screen to landscape orientation only
Remove all icons and replace with text labels site-wide

hints: Match the fix to the specific mechanism causing each problem — size, position, or adjacency — not a blanket redesign.
explanation: Each issue has a distinct mechanism and a targeted fix: the icon needs a bigger tappable area (not necessarily a bigger icon), the button needs repositioning to the thumb-reachable zone, and the adjacent destructive/routine pair needs separation or friction, not just resizing. The distractors are real design choices in the abstract but don't address the specific mechanism named in each case.

prompt: An expense-reporting tool's "submit expense" flow has four screens: receipt upload, amount + currency, category + cost-center dropdown, and a review-and-submit screen. Analyze whether this is a step-count problem or a styling problem, and justify your answer using what evidence you'd actually want to see before deciding.
hints: What pattern of drop-off would tell you it's step count versus one bad screen versus not a flow problem at all?
Consider which of the four screens' data could plausibly be merged onto one screen without hurting anything.
explanation: A defensible answer says the diagnosis requires evidence, not a guess from the description alone: if drop-off is even across all four screens and unmoved by past visual tweaks, that points at step count; if it spikes on one screen specifically, that screen has a distinct, fixable problem instead. Structurally, receipt upload, amount+currency, and category+cost-center are all short, related inputs that could plausibly collapse onto one screen (a single form with an upload field and a few inputs), leaving review-and-submit as a natural second and final step — cutting four screens to two without losing any required data.

prompt: A checkout flow asks for shipping address, then billing address, then a 'how did you hear about us' dropdown, before finally showing the order total and a pay button. True or false: all three of the first fields are load-bearing and none can be deferred.

config.statement: Shipping address, billing address, and 'how did you hear about us' are all required before a user can complete a purchase, so none of them can be deferred or removed from the pre-payment flow.
config.rubric: A full answer identifies that shipping and billing address are genuinely required to complete a purchase, but 'how did you hear about us' is marketing data that doesn't block payment and should be deferred (e.g. to a post-purchase screen) or made optional.

hints: Which of the three fields would actually block the transaction from being processable if left blank?
explanation: False. Shipping and billing address are genuinely required — the order can't ship or be charged without them. "How did you hear about us" is marketing attribution data with no bearing on whether the transaction can be processed; forcing it into the same required pre-payment flow adds a step (and a decision point where someone might abandon) for data that could just as easily be collected after payment, or made explicitly optional.

prompt: A solo developer's Next.js side project is deployed on Vercel's Hobby tier, getting modest traffic from friends testing it. They start charging users $5/month through the app. What does this trigger, per Vercel's terms?

options.text: The project is now commercial use, which the Hobby tier's terms don't cover — it needs to move to a paid Pro plan
Nothing changes — the Hobby tier has no restriction based on whether the app makes money
Vercel automatically takes a percentage of the app's revenue instead of a flat fee

hints: The Hobby tier's free status is scoped to personal, non-commercial use, not to a traffic threshold alone.
explanation: The Hobby tier is free for personal and non-commercial projects specifically — the moment an app is used commercially (charging users, running a business on it), Vercel's terms call for a paid plan regardless of how much or little traffic it gets. This is a real, load-bearing cost detail, not a technicality — deploying a paid product on Hobby is a terms violation, not a clever savings.

prompt: Explain, in your own words, why a bug introduced on a feature branch can't reach real briefdesk users just by virtue of Vercel's branch/domain model — without anyone having to remember to "be careful" or manually gate the deploy.
hints: Which domain does a non-main branch's deployment get, and does anything point real users at that domain?
Compare this to a setup with only one server and one URL, where every push — branch or not — updates the one thing users see.
explanation: A feature branch's deployment gets its own unique preview URL, structurally separate from the production domain — nothing about pushing to a branch changes what `briefdesk.app` serves. The safety isn't a discipline or a manual gate someone has to remember; it's a structural fact about which domain each branch's build is attached to. A bug only reaches real users once that branch is merged into the production branch and that build gets promoted to the production domain — an explicit, visible step, not an accident of pushing code.

prompt: A newly-added Vercel environment variable has only the "Production" box checked. A Development-environment `next dev` run and a Preview deployment both try to read it. What happens in each?

options.text: Both process.env reads return undefined — the variable simply doesn't exist outside the environment(s) it was explicitly scoped to
Both fall back automatically to the Production value, since it's the only one defined
Development works (local env vars always apply) but Preview fails

hints: Vercel doesn't treat 'Production' as a universal fallback for unchecked environments — each box genuinely gates whether the variable exists there.
explanation: Scoping in Vercel is exclusive, not a fallback hierarchy — a variable checked only for Production is genuinely absent from process.env in both Preview and Development builds unless it's separately configured (or a local .env.local supplies it for Development specifically). There's no automatic inheritance from Production to the other two.

prompt: Sort each credential into whether it's safe to share the same value across Production and Preview/Development, or whether it needs a separate non-production value.

items.text: A payment provider's secret key used to charge real customers
A metered AI API key billed per request
The production database's connection string
A public, read-only feature-flag service key with no spend or write access

hints: Ask, for each credential: can using it from a preview deployment or a local dev run cost money, corrupt real data, or trigger a real-world side effect?
explanation: Payment keys, metered API keys, and production database access all fail the test — using them from a non-production environment can spend real money, corrupt real user data, or process a real transaction, none of which a preview build or a local dev session should be able to do just by existing. A read-only, no-cost feature-flag key has none of those risks, so sharing it is a reasonable simplification rather than a hazard.

prompt: A feature works locally and in production but throws a 500 specifically on preview deployments. What should be checked first, before looking at the feature's own logic?

options.text: Whether every environment variable the feature depends on is actually scoped to include Preview in the dashboard
Whether the feature's algorithm has an edge case specific to preview URLs
Whether the reviewer's internet connection is unstable

hints: The code is identical across all three environments — what actually differs between them isn't the logic, it's what each environment's process.env contains.
explanation: Same code, different behavior by environment is the signature of an environment configuration gap, not a logic bug — the algorithm doesn't know or care which environment it's running in. Checking whether every required variable is actually scoped to Preview is a fast, high-probability first check before spending time auditing logic that's provably identical across all three environments.

prompt: A PR adds a "resend confirmation email" button to briefdesk's settings page. Describe specifically what a reviewer should do on the preview URL to actually check this PR, versus what checking only the diff would miss.
hints: Reading the diff would show the button's JSX and the handler calling an email-sending function — what does it not show about whether the email actually sends?
Consider what environment-scoped dependency an "email sending" feature likely has.
explanation: A reviewer should click the actual "resend confirmation email" button on the preview URL and confirm something real happens — a success message, and ideally that an email service call actually fires (visible in the email provider's logs, or at minimum no error). Reading the diff shows the button exists and calls a plausible-looking function, but can't show whether the email-sending service's API key is scoped to Preview, whether the email template renders correctly with real data, or whether the button is even reachable in the actual rendered layout — all things only running the real preview deployment reveals.

prompt: Why is promoting a previous Vercel deployment to production typically much faster than git revert + push?

options.text: The previous deployment is already a fully built artifact sitting in Vercel's history — promoting it just repoints the domain, with no rebuild step, while revert-and-push triggers a full build from scratch
Promoting a deployment uses a different, faster build system than a normal push does
There's no real speed difference — both take roughly the same amount of time

hints: What has to happen between 'git push' and a rebuilt site being live, that promoting an existing deployment skips entirely?
explanation: A rollback isn't a faster build — it's no build at all. Every deployment on Vercel is a complete, immutable artifact once it's built; promoting one to production is purely a routing change (which artifact does the domain point at), while git revert + push re-triggers the full build pipeline (install, build, upload) before anything changes for users.

prompt: A team rolls back a bad deploy at 3:00pm, confirms the site looks correct again, and moves on without touching git. True or false: the incident is fully resolved at this point.

config.statement: Once a rollback makes the live site look correct again, the incident is fully resolved and no further action in git is needed.
config.rubric: A full answer explains that main still points at the broken commit, so the very next deploy from any unrelated change will rebuild from that commit and silently undo the rollback — a git-level revert or fix is still required.

hints: Ask: what does main's git history look like right after the rollback? Does the rollback change git at all?
explanation: False. Rollback only changes what's live — it doesn't touch git. Main still has the broken commit at its tip, so the next deploy (from any teammate, for any unrelated reason) rebuilds from that same broken state and undoes the rollback without anyone intending to. The incident isn't closed until the bug is reverted or fixed in git and that fix has deployed, bringing production and git back into agreement.

prompt: Someone adds a CNAME record at the apex of example.com pointing at Vercel, instead of the A record Vercel's dashboard specified. What's the most likely outcome?

options.text: It may fail to resolve correctly or conflict with other required records (like MX for email) — apex domains generally can't use CNAME, which is why Vercel specifies an A record for them
It works identically to an A record — the two are interchangeable at any level of a domain
It makes the site load slightly faster, since CNAME resolution is more efficient

hints: Recall the structural DNS constraint on what can coexist at an apex domain.
explanation: A CNAME at the apex is a genuine DNS conflict, not a stylistic choice — it can prevent other required records (MX for email being the most common casualty) from working, and many registrars simply won't allow it. This is exactly why Vercel's own instructions specify an A record for apex domains and reserve CNAME for subdomains.

prompt: A team switches their app's primary domain from a *.vercel.app URL to a custom domain, verifies the homepage loads correctly, and considers the migration done. A week later, Stripe webhook events stop being received. Diagnose the likely cause and describe the audit step that would have caught it before launch.
hints: Stripe sends webhook events to a URL registered in Stripe's own dashboard — does changing your app's domain automatically update that?
This is the same category of problem as the OAuth redirect URI example from the lesson.
explanation: The likely cause: Stripe's webhook endpoint URL, registered in Stripe's dashboard, still points at the old *.vercel.app hostname — Stripe keeps sending events there (which may now 404, or simply go to a deployment nobody's monitoring) instead of the new custom domain. Changing DNS and the app's primary domain has no effect on a URL stored in a third-party system's own configuration. The audit step that would have caught it: checking every connected third-party service (payment webhooks, OAuth providers, CORS configs, email templates) for hardcoded references to the old domain, not just confirming the homepage itself loads correctly on the new one.

prompt: A team pushes to a feature branch and expects it to appear at their production domain. Nothing changes at that domain. What's the correct explanation?

options.text: Only the connected production branch (usually main) deploys to the production domain — other branches get their own separate preview URLs, working as intended
The deploy silently failed and needs to be retried
Vercel requires a manual 'promote' click for every single push, including to main

hints: Recall the two-domain model: production tracks one specific branch, everything else gets its own preview URL.
explanation: This is expected behavior, not a failure — a non-production branch is never meant to reach the production domain automatically. It gets its own preview deployment and URL instead, which is the entire mechanism that keeps in-progress work from reaching real users.

prompt: A newly added STRIPE_SECRET_KEY variable in Vercel has only 'Production' checked. A developer runs the app locally with `next dev` and the Stripe client throws 'key not defined'. Why does this fail locally too, not just on preview?

options.text: Local dev reads from .env.local, a separate file entirely — Vercel's dashboard scoping (Production/Preview/Development) has no effect on local runs unless the value is also added to .env.local
Vercel's Development scope and local .env.local are the same thing, so checking 'Development' in the dashboard would have fixed local dev too
Local dev always requires re-authenticating with Vercel's CLI before env vars work

hints: Vercel's Development-scoped variables apply to `vercel dev`, not necessarily to `next dev` run directly against a local .env.local.
explanation: A plain `next dev` reads environment variables from `.env.local` on disk, which is entirely separate from what's configured in Vercel's dashboard — checking 'Development' in the dashboard affects `vercel dev` (Vercel's own local-dev proxy) or values pulled via `vercel env pull`, not a bare `next dev` with no `.env.local` entry for that key. The fix here is adding the key to `.env.local` directly, not just checking a box in the dashboard.

prompt: A bad deploy just broke a live feature for real users. Put the incident-response steps in the correct order.

items: Confirm the bug is real and live, not a false alarm
Promote the last known-good deployment to production (rollback)
Confirm the rollback actually fixed the live symptom
Fix or revert the bug in git, on its own PR
Let the fix deploy normally, bringing git and production back into agreement

hints: Rollback comes before the git-level fix, not after — speed matters more than correctness-of-process in the first step of a live incident.
explanation: Confirm first (don't roll back based on a false report), roll back immediately for speed, verify the rollback actually worked, then address the root cause in git so the next deploy doesn't undo the rollback, then let that proper fix ship. Skipping straight to a git-level fix as the first step (skipping rollback) leaves users seeing the broken behavior for the full duration of a rebuild, which is exactly the delay this module's rollback lesson warns against.

prompt: A reviewer approves a PR after reading the diff carefully, without opening the preview URL. The PR turns out to break a feature that depends on a Preview-scoped environment variable that was never actually configured. What would opening the preview URL have caught that the diff review missed?

options.text: The actual runtime failure — an env-dependent feature failing in the running preview deployment, which is invisible from reading code that looks correct
Nothing — a careful diff review is equivalent to checking the preview URL
Only cosmetic issues like font choices, not functional bugs

hints: A missing environment variable isn't visible in a code diff at all — the code correctly references process.env.SOMETHING; the absence is only visible at runtime.
explanation: A missing or misscoped environment variable produces code that looks entirely correct in a diff — the bug only exists at runtime, in a specific environment, which a diff can't represent at all. This is exactly why exercising the actual feature on the real preview URL catches a category of bug that reading code, however carefully, structurally cannot.

prompt: Match each deployment symptom to its most likely cause.

pairs.left: A feature works in production and locally, but throws 'undefined' errors only on preview URLs
pairs.right: An environment variable scoped to Production (and local .env.local) but never checked for Preview

pairs.left: A live incident is fixed by rollback, then reappears an hour later after an unrelated deploy
pairs.right: The buggy commit was never reverted in git, so the next deploy rebuilt from it

pairs.left: 'Sign in with Google' fails only after switching to a custom domain
pairs.right: The OAuth redirect URI registered with the provider still lists the old *.vercel.app URL

right: The Vercel account has exceeded its Hobby-tier bandwidth limit
A DNS record was configured as CNAME instead of A at the apex domain

hints: Match each symptom to the specific mechanism from this module's lessons that produces exactly that pattern.
explanation: Each symptom has a distinct, diagnosable mechanism covered in this module: environment scoping gaps produce environment-specific failures with identical code; an un-reverted git commit means a rollback's fix is temporary until the next unrelated deploy; and third-party services (like OAuth providers) don't automatically learn about a domain change, so their stored redirect URI goes stale. The distractors are real possible issues but don't match the specific symptom pattern described.

prompt: A team's Stripe webhook stops receiving events two weeks after they switched their app to a custom domain. List every place you'd check, in the order you'd check them, before concluding the webhook itself is broken.
hints: Start from the fact that the app worked fine on the old domain — what's different now, structurally, that a domain switch wouldn't automatically fix?
Consider what Stripe's dashboard has stored versus what your app's DNS or code changed.
explanation: A reasonable order: (1) check Stripe's dashboard for the webhook endpoint URL it's actually configured to call — this is the single most likely culprit, since it's a value stored in a third-party system that a domain switch doesn't automatically update; (2) confirm the new domain's route that handles the webhook actually exists and responds correctly if hit directly; (3) check Stripe's webhook delivery logs for the specific error (404, timeout, signature mismatch) rather than guessing; (4) only after ruling those out, suspect an actual bug in the webhook handler itself. The domain-switch context strongly suggests the stored URL in Stripe's dashboard is the cause, per this module's custom-domain lesson.

prompt: A solo developer deploys a free personal project on Vercel's Hobby tier and later starts accepting paid subscriptions through it. True or false: as long as traffic stays under the Hobby tier's bandwidth limit, no plan change is required.

config.statement: Staying under the Hobby tier's bandwidth limit is sufficient to keep using it once the project starts generating commercial revenue.
config.rubric: A full answer explains that the Hobby tier's eligibility is based on commercial use, not traffic volume alone — accepting payments makes the project commercial regardless of how little bandwidth it uses.

hints: Recall what specifically triggers the need for a Pro plan — is it a usage threshold, or a use-case category?
explanation: False. The Hobby tier's terms are scoped to personal, non-commercial use — the qualifying factor is what the project is (commercial or not), not how much bandwidth or traffic it generates. A project charging real subscribers needs a paid plan the moment it starts doing that, independent of whether its actual usage numbers would otherwise fit comfortably within Hobby's limits.

prompt: A screen fetches a list and renders it with `const [items, setItems] = useState([]); ...; return <List items={items} />;` and nothing else. For a brand-new account that genuinely has zero items, and for the same account before the fetch has resolved, what does the user see in each case?

options.text: The identical empty rendering in both cases — there's no status value distinguishing 'still loading' from 'loaded, genuinely empty'
A default loading spinner appears automatically before the fetch resolves, then an empty-state message once it's confirmed empty
React throws a warning in the console distinguishing the two cases, even though the visual rendering is the same

hints: `items` is `[]` in both situations — ask what other piece of state, if any, actually changes between them.
explanation: Both situations render `<List items={[]} />` — identical output — because nothing in this code tracks whether the fetch is still in flight versus already resolved. React doesn't add a default spinner or distinguish these cases on its own; that requires an explicit status value the developer tracks themselves, which is exactly what's missing here.

prompt: A junior developer says: "Our fetch has a .catch that sets an error flag, so we're covering all the states already." Their code is: `fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).then(setData).catch(() => setError(true))`, with `data` initialized to `[]`. Explain what's still missing, specifically.
hints: Consider what `r.ok` being false (a 404 or 500 status) actually does inside a `.then(r => r.json())` chain — does it reject the promise on its own?
Separately: even with the catch in place, can 'still loading' still be confused with something else here?
explanation: Two gaps remain. First, `fetch` only rejects on a genuine network failure — a 404 or 500 response is still a 'successful' fetch as far as the Promise chain is concerned, so `r.json()` runs against an error body and the `.catch` never fires for a failed HTTP status; that needs an explicit `if (!r.ok) throw new Error()` before parsing. Second, `data` still starts as `[]` with no separate loading flag, so 'still fetching' and 'loaded, genuinely empty' still render identically even with the error path handled — the catch alone doesn't add the missing loading/empty distinction from this lesson's main point.

prompt: briefdesk's brief-generation route returns a 400 status when clientNotes exceeds the character limit. The frontend currently shows the same generic 'Something went wrong. Try again.' message for every non-2xx response, with a retry button. What's the concrete problem with wiring the 400 case to that same message and button?

options.text: Clicking 'Try again' resends the identical oversized request, which fails identically — the message also never tells the user their input is the actual problem, or by how much it's over the limit
400 status codes should never be handled on the frontend at all, only logged server-side
The message's wording is fine; the real problem is that a 400 status should be styled in orange instead of red

hints: What does clicking the retry button actually do to the request that just failed — does anything about it change?
explanation: A retry button on a validation failure resends the exact same request with the exact same oversized input, producing the exact same 400 every time — it's not just unhelpful, it actively teaches the user the app is broken. The fix is a message naming the specific limit and how far over it the input is, paired with an action that lets the user fix the input directly rather than repeat the failing request.

prompt: Sort each failure by the response it should get: an immediate retry button, a 'fix your input' action (no retry), or an honest 'try again shortly' message with no immediate retry.

items.text: The browser's fetch itself throws because the connection dropped mid-request
The server returns a 400 because a required field was left blank
The server returns a 502 because the AI provider it depends on is currently down
The server returns a 400 because a file exceeds the upload size limit

hints: For each one, ask: does clicking retry with the exact same request have any real chance of succeeding right now?
explanation: A dropped connection is transient and unrelated to the request's content — an immediate retry is likely to work. A missing field or an oversized file is a property of the input itself — retrying without changing the input reproduces the identical failure, so the fix belongs to the user correcting their input, not a retry button. A dependency outage means the request's content was never the issue, but an immediate retry is also unlikely to help right this second — the honest response acknowledges the outage rather than looping retries against a service that's still down.

prompt: A dashboard combines three fetches with `Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB(), fetchC()])` inside one try/catch, with a single `status` variable set in the catch block. fetchB times out; fetchA and fetchC both succeed. What renders?

options.text: The catch block fires, status becomes 'error', and the whole dashboard shows an error state — the successful results from fetchA and fetchC are discarded, not just fetchB's
fetchA and fetchC render normally, and only the section depending on fetchB shows an error, with no code changes needed
Promise.all automatically retries fetchB up to three times before giving up

hints: Promise.all rejects the instant any one of its promises rejects — what happens to the ones that already resolved successfully at that point?
explanation: Promise.all is all-or-nothing: the moment fetchB's promise rejects, the whole Promise.all rejects too, and the values fetchA and fetchC already resolved with are never delivered to any `.then` — they're simply discarded. With one shared `status` variable set only in the catch block, the entire dashboard renders as failed even though two-thirds of its data loaded successfully.

prompt: briefdesk's dashboard has a client list (primary content) and a small 'recently viewed' sidebar (a minor convenience, rarely checked, rebuilt from a cheap local cache if it fails). Describe how each section's failure should actually be handled, and why they shouldn't get identical treatment.
hints: Ask, for each section: if it silently failed and nobody said anything, would the user walk away believing something false about their own data?
